d.title: The bug src layout prevents is testing the wrong copy of your code
d.caption: **Without it, the project root is on `sys.path`, so `import mypackage` finds the source directory rather than the installed package — and the tests pass against code that was never installed.** Which hides a whole class of packaging error: **a missing `__init__.py`, a file excluded from the wheel, a data file that is not package data.** With a `src/` directory the import can only resolve to the installed copy, **so the tests exercise what a user would get, and a packaging mistake fails in CI rather than on first install.**

nodes.label: The project root is on sys.path
So packaging errors are invisible
nodes.sub: a file missing from the wheel

nodes.label: And the mistake fails in CI
nodes.sub: not on a user's first install

d.title: A cycle is a design signal, not an import problem
d.caption: **Reaching for `TYPE_CHECKING` first hides the message**, which is that two modules each need something the other has — so one of them is in the wrong place. The three honest fixes, in order of preference: **move the shared thing into a third module that both import, move the function to the module that owns the data it uses, or invert the dependency so the lower layer declares a protocol the higher one satisfies.** `TYPE_CHECKING` is correct for a genuine annotation-only cycle, **and wrong as a first response, because the cycle will come back as a runtime one.**

nodes.label: A imports B, B imports A
Move the shared thing to a third module
Or move the function to the data's owner
Or invert it with a Protocol

d.title: A rule enforced only in review is a rule that survives until a busy week
d.caption: **These three contracts are the whole mechanism, and all three are machine-checkable** — which is the point, because architecture that depends on everyone remembering is architecture that erodes silently. **`import-linter` declares the layers and fails the build on a violation; `ruff`'s banned-import rules stop a specific module reaching a specific other one; and a dependency test asserts the domain package imports nothing from the framework.** The last is the cheapest: **one test, and it catches the import that a reviewer would have had to notice.**

nodes.label: A test: domain imports no framework

d.title: Six places to put a secret, three of which are never
d.caption: **A repository is never, because git history is permanent and a rotation does not remove it** — the secret stays in every clone forever. A Docker `ENV` is never, **because image layers are readable by anyone who can pull it.** And a URL is never, **because URLs appear in access logs, proxies and browser history.** The useful part is the top of the ladder: **a mounted file beats an environment variable — it is not in `/proc/*/environ` and it can be rotated without a restart** — and a secret manager with a short-lived token adds audit and revocation.

d.title: Build this before you need it
d.caption: **Rotating under pressure — after a leak — is when you discover that your application reads the secret once at startup, that two services share it, and that nothing accepts two values at the same time.** Which is why the capability matters more than the schedule: **support two valid keys simultaneously, so a rotation is two deploys rather than an outage**, and **re-read the secret rather than caching it at import**, so the second deploy is not required at all. And the test worth having: **rotate in staging on a timer, so the path is exercised before an incident uses it.**

nodes.label: You discover: read once at startup
Support TWO valid keys at once
Rotate in staging on a timer

d.title: Cardinality is the column that decides what goes where
d.caption: **Logs take any field at unlimited cardinality — a user id, a request id, an order number — and metrics do not.** A metric label with high cardinality multiplies the stored time series: **one label with 10,000 user ids is 10,000 series per metric**, which is how a monitoring bill and then a monitoring outage happen. So the division is mechanical rather than stylistic: **identifiers go in logs and traces, and metrics carry only bounded labels** — status code, endpoint, region. Traces sit between them: **high cardinality, and sampled, so the cost is bounded by the sample rate.**

where the time went, across services

d.title: Conflating liveness and readiness is a classic outage amplifier
d.caption: **A liveness probe that checks the database restarts every replica when the database is briefly slow** — so a recoverable dependency blip becomes a full restart storm, and the restarts make the database slower. The division: **liveness asks “is this process wedged” and must check nothing external; readiness asks “can this replica serve traffic now” and may check dependencies**, because its failure removes the replica from the load balancer instead of killing it. And for alerts: **page on symptoms a user feels, not on causes** — error rate and latency, not CPU.

nodes.label: A brief blip restarts every replica
And page on symptoms, not causes
nodes.sub: error rate and latency, not CPU

d.title: `.git-blame-ignore-revs` is the step people skip
d.caption: **Without it, a formatting commit makes `git blame` useless on every line it touched** — so the one-off reformat that was supposed to end style review costs you the history of the whole file, permanently. The adoption order that works on a legacy codebase: **format everything in one commit, record that commit's hash in `.git-blame-ignore-revs`, then turn on the checks.** And for types, the equivalent is per-module strictness: **`disallow_untyped_defs` on the modules you have annotated and nothing elsewhere**, so the ratchet only tightens.

d.title: `PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1` is not optional
d.caption: **Without it stdout is block-buffered when not a TTY, so logs appear in chunks minutes late — or not at all when the container is killed**, which is precisely the moment you needed them. The rest of the Dockerfile is layer ordering: **copy the lock file and install before copying the source, so a code change does not invalidate the dependency layer.** And the two that reduce what an attacker gets: **a non-root `USER`, and a multi-stage build so the compiler and the build dependencies never reach the final image.**

nodes.label: Lock file and install BEFORE the source
nodes.sub: so code changes keep the cache

nodes.label: Multi-stage: no compiler in the final image

d.title: Alpine is 50 MB and compiles your wheels from source
d.caption: **musl libc means many wheels simply do not exist for it — so a build that is 130 MB and thirty seconds on slim becomes 50 MB and fifteen minutes on alpine**, with a compiler in the image unless you stage it out. Which is why **slim is the default choice: Debian, glibc, and wheels just work.** The two ends are for specific reasons: **the full image is ~1.0 GB of attack surface you do not need**, and **distroless has no shell and no package manager — secure, and hard to debug when you need to.**

state: far more attack surface than needed
no shell - secure, hard to debug

d.title: `hashFiles('requirements.txt')` on an unpinned file is a false key
d.caption: **The file is unchanged, the resolved versions are not — so the cache hits and you install yesterday's resolution, or it hits and you install something different from what the last build tested.** Which is the general shape of a cache-key bug: **the key must cover everything that affects the result.** For a lock file the hash is correct, because the lock file *is* the resolution. And the second rule: **include the Python version and the platform in the key**, since a wheel cache from 3.11 on x86 is not valid for 3.12 on arm.

nodes.label: The key must cover what affects the result

d.title: Nine gates, and the two that should not block are the ones people add first
d.caption: **A total coverage threshold of 80% encourages tests of getters rather than of behaviour** — it is satisfiable by the least valuable tests available, which is why a **decrease** is the gate worth having instead. And **“every dependency current” is noise: it fails builds for a patch release nobody needed**, so batch upgrades on a schedule. The seven that should block are all cheap and all catch something specific — **including the migration check, because a non-concurrent index build is an outage, not a slow deploy.**

d.title: A rollback that requires thought is not a rollback
d.caption: **The previous digest is known at deploy time, so restoring it is one command that needs no decision and no investigation** — which is the only property that matters at 3am. The constraint that makes it true is the one people discover too late: **the database must be compatible with both versions, so a migration that drops a column cannot be rolled back by redeploying the old image.** Hence the sequence: **expand, deploy, contract** — add the column, ship code that writes both, and only remove the old one after the rollback window has closed.

nodes.label: Unless a migration dropped a column
nodes.sub: then the old image cannot run

d.title: Seven questions, and the bad answers are specific enough to check
d.caption: **“One direct dependency becomes forty transitive” is the one with compounding cost — forty packages to audit, forty to update, forty with their own maintainers.** And the last is the one people never ask: **a `setup.py` doing network I/O runs code at install time, so `pip install` is arbitrary code execution on your build machine** — which is why the wheel-only install is worth enforcing. The pair worth weighing together: **using one function out of two hundred, when you could write thirty lines yourself.**

d.title: A CVSS score is not a priority
d.caption: **A critical vulnerability in a code path you never execute is a patch to schedule; a medium one in your authentication path is tonight's work** — and the scanner cannot tell them apart, because it scores the vulnerability rather than your exposure to it. So the triage question is reachability: **do we call the affected function, is the input attacker-controlled, and is the path reachable without authentication?** Which is why **a scanner that blocks on severity alone trains people to add blanket ignores** — and a blanket ignore hides the one that mattered.

nodes.label: Critical, in code you never call
Blocking on severity alone
nodes.sub: trains people to add blanket ignores

d.title: An SBOM is inventory, not protection
d.caption: **Its whole value is answering the exposure question quickly** — when a CVE lands in a transitive dependency, the difference between a ten-minute answer and a two-day audit is whether you generated one. Which is also its limit: **it prevents nothing, and a complete SBOM for a vulnerable system is still a vulnerable system.** Provenance is the other half and answers a different question: **a signed attestation says *this* artifact came from *that* commit through *that* pipeline**, so an image nobody can trace to a build is one you should not deploy.

nodes.label: An SBOM lists what is inside
An untraceable image is undeployable
nodes.sub: which is the policy it enables

d.title: A missing timeout is not “no timeout” — it is the longest one in the stack
d.caption: **Something will eventually give up — a load balancer at 60 seconds, a kernel socket timeout, a client that reconnects — and until then your worker is held.** So the real question is whether *you* chose the number or inherited it. The rule that makes a stack coherent: **each layer's timeout must be shorter than the layer that calls it**, or an inner retry outlives the outer request and does work nobody is waiting for. And the set to configure explicitly: **connect, read, total, and the pool checkout** — because a connect timeout alone leaves a slow response unbounded.

nodes.label: No timeout set
nodes.sub: means the longest in the stack

nodes.label: And your worker is held until then
Each layer shorter than its caller
nodes.sub: or a retry outlives the request

nodes.label: Set connect, read, total and pool
Connect alone leaves the read unbounded

d.title: Seven questions, and the last two are usually where the answer is
d.caption: **`py-spy dump` needs no restart and adds no overhead, which is what makes it the first command** — you get the stack of a wedged production process without changing anything. But the two rows at the bottom are the ones people reach for last and should reach for early: **`pg_stat_activity` is often the real answer**, because a Python process that looks stuck is usually waiting on a query, and **`ss -tanp` shows connection states**, where a pile of `CLOSE_WAIT` means your code is not closing sockets it was handed.

steps.code: what is it doing right now?

d.title: Four failure shapes, recognisable by their curve before you read any code
d.caption: **The curve narrows the hypothesis before you look at anything** — a sudden step at a deploy time is a change you made, a slow ramp over hours is a leak or an unbounded queue, a daily spike is a scheduled job, and a sawtooth is a restart loop masking something. Which matters because of the rule next to it: **a hypothesis must be falsifiable and cheap** — “the database is slow” is neither, and “`pg_stat_activity` will show queries waiting on a lock” is both, **and takes ten seconds to settle.**

d.title: One transaction holding one network call
d.caption: **The incident trail ends at a bug small enough to state in a sentence: a transaction left open across an HTTP call to a payment provider.** Which is 13.4's rule violated once, and the consequence compounds exactly as that lesson predicts — **the provider slowed, every request held a pooled connection and a row lock for the duration, the pool exhausted, and the symptom was reported as “the site is down”.** The general lesson from the trail: **the metric told you *when*, `py-spy` told you *where*, and `pg_stat_activity` told you *why*** — three tools, in that order.

nodes.label: A transaction open across an HTTP call
Every request held a connection and a lock
Metric when, py-spy where, pg_stat why

d.title: What makes a postmortem worth writing
d.caption: **A timeline with timestamps, so the detection gap is visible as a number rather than an impression** — the gap between the first error and the first alert is usually the most actionable thing in the document. Then: **contributing factors in the plural, because a single root cause is almost always a simplification**, and **action items with an owner and a date, because the ones without either do not happen.** And the property that determines whether anyone writes the next one: **blameless — the question is what made this easy to do, not who did it.**

nodes.sub: the detection gap as a number

d.title: A seam you do not use is a cost with no benefit
d.caption: **Every abstraction adds a layer to read through, so add one when you have a second implementation or a test that needs it — not in anticipation.** Which is the honest version of “design for change”: **the repository interface with exactly one implementation is a file that every reader must open and that no caller benefits from.** And the counter-rule that keeps it from becoming an excuse: **a seam is cheap to add later only if the call sites are few** — so the thing to watch is not the abstraction, it is how many places would have to change.

nodes.label: Add it when there is a second
nodes.sub: or a test that needs it

nodes.label: Cheap to add later IF call sites are few

d.title: Record the alternatives, not just the choice
d.caption: **The value is telling a future reader what was already thought about** — a decision record listing only the decision invites someone to re-propose the option you rejected for a good reason, and they will do it eighteen months later with no way to know. So the shape that pays: **context, the options considered, the decision, and the consequences you accepted.** And the discipline that keeps them useful: **record the decision when it is made, not when it is questioned** — because the reasoning is only available while it is still fresh.

nodes.label: A record listing only the decision
Written when the decision is made
Because the reasoning is only fresh once

d.title: Four quadrants, and only two of them are debt
d.caption: **“Ship it now, refactor after launch” is deliberate and prudent — fine, and it needs a recorded trigger, because debt with no trigger is a decision that quietly became permanent.** “Now we know how it should be structured” is inadvertent and prudent, **and it is simply normal: refactor as you learn.** The other two are not debt at all, which is the useful part of the model: **“we don't have time for tests” is damage, and “what's a repository pattern?” is a learning problem** — and calling either one debt hides what to do about it.

state: 'now we know how it should be'
